title: Cyrus and the Glasshouse
premise: Coral Whitlock, a translator who has spent his life rendering other people's words while hoarding his own, is summoned to the glasshouse estate of Emeric Voss, the last fluent speaker of Lissene, the dying language of Coral's childhood. Voss offers to teach him everything before he dies—but the lessons reveal that Coral's grandmother, once Voss's closest collaborator, was erased from the language's official history by Voss himself. As Coral's fluency grows, so does his fury, and he must choose between preserving a language and honoring the woman it was stolen from. In the end, Coral records Voss's confession in Lissene, teaches the language forward through his own students with his grandmother's name restored at its center, and finally speaks aloud—at her grave—the goodbye he owed her for thirty years.
about_author: Ansel Brightwater is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent a decade transcribing testimony in languages not their own. They live near a botanical conservatory and write about the words people refuse to say.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. We meet him cataloguing his shrinking Lissene vocabulary in a worn notebook—each borrowed word replacing one he can no longer recall. A letter arrives from Emeric Voss requesting his presence as final student. Coral almost declines; the language is tangled with his silent grandmother. Beat: reluctant hope stirring under long habit of silence.

chapters.title: Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. He arrives at Voss's estate—a Victorian greenhouse converted into a library of recordings, dictionaries, and dead speakers' letters. Voss is imperious, brilliant, and dying. The first lesson begins: naming things. Coral recognizes his grandmother's handwriting on old field notes and says nothing. Beat: wonder shadowed by a first crack of suspicion.

chapters.title: Lessons in Dying
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, alternating with excerpts from Voss's teaching journal. Daily immersion: songs, curses, lullabies. Coral's fluency returns faster than expected, unsettling them both. Voss tests him cruelly, demanding perfection. Coral learns Voss's health is failing faster than admitted. Beat: intimacy forming between teacher and student, built on unequal ground.

chapters.title: What the Field Notes Say
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Alone in the archive at night, Coral finds his grandmother Maren's original transcriptions—the true grammar beneath Voss's published version, quietly corrected, then credited to him alone. Her name appears only as 'informant.' Coral confronts the notebook inventory: all the things she never said either. Beat: betrayal crystallizing into purpose.

chapters.title: The Erasure
chapters.summary: Voss's POV, decades earlier. Young Emeric and Maren documenting Lissene together as equals, lovers perhaps, until institutional pressure and ambition make her an embarrassment—an uncredentialed village woman. He rewrites the record, tells himself it's for the language's survival. Beat: corruption shown as a series of small reasonable choices.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Conservatory
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. He accuses Voss in Lissene—the first time the accusation could only be made in the stolen tongue. Voss neither denies nor apologizes; he argues the language would have died with her credit intact. Coral nearly walks out, but realizes leaving means Maren's version dies too. Beat: rage held in check by duty.

chapters.title: Bargaining with a Dying Man
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral proposes terms: he will complete the lessons and preserve Voss's recordings, but the new grammar will carry Maren's corrections and her name. Voss resists, weakens, bargains, stalls. His condition deteriorates mid-lesson; Coral finishes dictating a story in Voss's voice, realizing he now knows the language better than its last speaker. Beat: power shifting hands.

chapters.title: Confession
chapters.summary: Dual POV converging. Coral brings a recorder to Voss's bedside and asks—not for apology but for testimony—in Lissene. Voss speaks the truth of Maren's erasure, the full recording, unedited, in the language itself. It is both restitution and theft's final admission. Beat: catharsis without absolution; Voss dies that night.

chapters.title: Restoration
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Months later: Coral compiles the restored grammar, Maren Whitlock named as co-author on every page. He begins teaching a small class of diaspora learners, including a girl who reminds him of himself. The inventory notebook becomes a teaching text—unsaid things finally said. Beat: grief transmuted into inheritance rightly given.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. At Maren's grave, Coral delivers the goodbye he has carried for thirty years—in full Lissene, fluent and unbroken, with his students standing behind him listening. The language lives because it was taken, and now because it was returned. Final image: the girl asking him how to say 'begin.' Beat: quiet, earned resolution.
